analysis.one_liner: Lets public water systems sue polluters and pesticide makers to recover the cost of treating contaminated drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to give public water utilities a new right to sue in federal court. If a utility had to spend money treating or monitoring contaminated source water, it could recover those costs from anyone whose negligence caused or contributed to the contamination, and — in the case of pesticides — directly from the product's manufacturer or importer, without proving negligence. Normal, correctly applied fertilizer and pesticide use would have been exempt, as would federally permitted releases and contributors responsible for only small amounts.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of public water systems — meaning the communities they serve — would gain a new federal cause of action to shift the costs of treating and monitoring contaminated drinking water onto the parties responsible. Households would benefit indirectly if utility cleanup costs, normally paid through water rates, were recovered from polluters instead.

how_it_helps.text: Public water systems — and by extension the households that pay their rates — could sue negligent parties to recover what they spend treating or monitoring contaminated source water, instead of absorbing those costs in water bills.

For pesticide contamination specifically, the bill creates a special cause of action against manufacturers and importers, making them pay the portion of treatment costs attributable to their products without the system having to prove negligence.

analysis.who_pays: Negligent polluters and, for pesticide contamination, manufacturers and importers of FIFRA-regulated chemicals would bear the cost of reimbursing treatment and monitoring expenses. Exemptions for lawful fertilizer and pesticide application and small contributions would narrow who actually pays.

drawbacks.text: Farmers and applicators are exempt when they follow label instructions, so the most common routes of agricultural runoff — normal fertilizer and pesticide application — would not generate liability; the bill aims only at negligent parties and manufacturers/importers.

A court can shield anyone found to have caused only a small portion of the contamination, and federally permitted releases are excluded, so many polluters would escape payment and water systems would bear the litigation burden of proving attribution.

If manufacturers had to reimburse treatment costs, some of that liability could ultimately be passed through to consumers in product prices, and the exemptions limit how much of the public's decontamination bill would actually be recovered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift a real, ongoing cost — treating farm and industrial chemicals out of drinking water — from ratepayers to the companies whose products caused it, which is a straightforward fairness improvement. The strongest objections are the carve-outs: ordinary pesticide and fertilizer use is exempt when label directions are followed, and small contributors are shielded, so recovery would be limited to the clearest cases and chemical makers would still dodge much of the bill. It also leaves water systems to fund and win lawsuits rather than simply getting clean sources. The bill was never debated or voted on, so none of this was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to House committees and its health subcommittee in June 1996, and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Torricelli (D-NJ), joined by Rep. Frank Pallone and three other Democratic cosponsors, introduced the bill on June 13, 1996.
The House referred it to the Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, and on June 21, 1996 its Commerce subcommittee reference became the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never left subcommittee and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 without the bill receiving a hearing or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Polluters and pesticide manufacturers are better off, since they faced no new liability, and water ratepayers continue to pay cleanup costs.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Joined Torricelli in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 21, 1996 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Agricultural chemical industry
against.role: Pesticide manufacturers and farm-chemical trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed pesticide-manufacturer liability legislation of this kind in the 104th Congress as the Safe Drinking Water Act was being reauthorized.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one's position was ever recorded on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would make pesticide and FIFRA-regulated chemical makers and importers directly liable for water systems' treatment and monitoring costs attributable to their products, without requiring proof of negligence. This is exactly the industry the bill was written to reach.

industries.industry: Fertilizer producers and negligent industrial polluters
industries.note: Negligent contributors to source-water contamination would have to reimburse treatment costs. Normal, instruction-following fertilizer application is exempted, so liability would attach mainly where use violated instructions or the law.

industries.industry: Public water utilities and their ratepayers
industries.note: Utilities could recover decontamination and monitoring costs from polluters rather than passing them to customers through rates. The bill also explicitly preserves utilities' rights to sue under other laws.
